May I say-and I am sure hon. members will be relieved when I add "in conclusion"- that there are only three ways in which the prices of goods can be fixed.
The first is by competition. A witness before the joint committee told us that as to the great majority of goods in Canada their prices, their wholesale and retail mark-ups, were determined by competition. For example, this is the case with over 95 per cent of the grocery trade and over 92 per cent of the hardware trade.
The second way is by government control. I think most of us agree that in our free Canadian economy government interference in business should be kept to a minimum and therefore price fixing by the government should be avoided if possible.
The third way that prices can be fixed is by the control of private interests either in the form of (a) price fixing combines, which are quite illegal and indeed criminal under the existing law, or (b) by resale price maintenance which in certain forms and under certain circumstances is also illegal under the existing law. It is for the purpose of making all forms of resale price maintenance illegal that the present bill is being introduced.
I suggest that if this parliament and this government allow price competition amongst wholesalers and retailers to continue to be eliminated by resale price maintenance in certain trades, we shall have to answer four vital and searching questions by the Canadian consumers and by the many hundreds of thousands-some people will say millions- of little fellows amongst these consumers. These consumers being largely unorganized and unprotected, are forced to look for justice in this matter to this parliament and this government. Judging by what some of them have written and told me, I think this is what they are saying to us: We are little fellows ourselves, so naturally we are on the side of the little fellow in the retail business. All we ask is that he work as hard and plan as carefully as we must do in our walk of life. But is there one good reason why the independent retailer, the little fellow, who will not take the trouble to make himself reasonably efficient-not extremely efficient; just reasonably efficient-should be protected under resale price maintenance by profit margins which, at our expense, will provide for the reasonably efficient merchants profits which they do not need, and in some cases do not wish to take, but which resale price maintenance compels them to take? That, they would say, is question No. 1: Is there one good reason for this sort of protection?
Then I think they would say to us: Our second question is this. Can anyone bring

forward a reason why the little fellow in some trades needs heavy protection from resale price maintenance whereas in the grocery and hardware trades, for example-and there are others-the independent dealers, including all the little fellows, when they are reasonably efficient have demonstrated for many years that they can keep their share of the retail trade and the profits in it, against all competition?
The third question they would ask is this: If the government will not control prices itself, is there any good reason why wholesale and retail profit mark-ups should be left to a substantial extent under the private control of manufacturers?
The fourth and final question which they would ask of this parliament is this: Is it reasonable to expect the Canadian people as consumers to tolerate indefinitely the practice of resale price maintenance whereby the cost of distribution of goods and the prices of the goods themselves are fixed by the manufacturers without the safeguard of price competition amongst wholesalers and retailers?
These are all very just questions. They are all questions to which the men and women in Canada who are consumers are entitled to an answer. In the government's view the answer to every one of those questions is: No, there is no good reason; and these negative answers, in- our view, constitute one of the strongest arguments in support of the present bill.
This bill proposes to make it an offence for a manufacturer or a dealer to prescribe fixed or minimum resale prices. He may still prescribe and enforce maximum resale prices. He may also indicate resale prices as long as he does not do so in such a way as to require or induce another person to maintain them. The man who wishes to be law-abiding in this regard, I suggest, will not have any trouble at all in avoiding any action which could be interpreted as requiring or inducing another person to maintain prices.

The whole course followed by the government in connection with this legislation has been as extraordinary as has been the spectacle we have just witnessed. That they themselves are unconvinced of the merits of the bill and that, if they press it through

to a conclusion, they are doing so for nothing more than party political purposes, was nowhere more clearly demonstrated than in the tactics they have followed during the whole of this session. At every turn since the beginning of the session in October they have attempted to choke off discussion on the merits of the proposal to outlaw price maintenance.
The speech from the throne announced the proposal to bring in legislation at this session. Nothing was done about that matter and no further reference was made to it until the beginning of November, when it was announced that it was intended to refer it to a committee. The committee was not set up for a week after that announcement was made. The committee's sittings were limited. An artificial termination date was placed upon them. The evidence which that committee was allowed to receive and consider was curtailed. But most reprehensible of all in connection with this extremely important matter has been the delay of a whole week at this stage, after the presenting of its report by the committee and the reference of the matter back to the house a week ago last Friday, before proceeding with this legislation in the house in the obvious hope, Mr. Speaker, that the approach of Christmas and the human desire on the part of the members to rejoin their families would have the result that those opposed to the legislation-and I may say that they are to be found on both sides of this house-would be induced to leave; and thus the bill would, they hoped, enjoy in the house that cursory and inadequate examination only which the government majority had allowed it in committee, and its passage would, they hoped, be expedited.
Never was a more serious and far-reaching step affecting some 700,000 Canadians directly engaged in or dependent on the retail trade more summarily and inadequately treated- and thus treated for political purposes only. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the anxiety of the minister not to deal with the merits of the matter in the house but to play politics and to build up political pressure outside the house was nowhere more clearly demonstrated than in the fact that, even after this long delay before bringing the bill back into the house and dealing with it, his speech of this evening was reproduced in the press before it was delivered in the house.

I am not holding the minister accountable for whether it appeared in one paper or not. I am merely referring to the fact that the whole course of action followed by the government with respect to this legislation has had the result that the matter has been dealt with on a political basis in the country before there was ever an opportunity for discussion on the merits in the house because its introduction here has been held up in the hope Christmas would take members home so the bill would slip through. I think what the minister has just said verifies that statement.
As to the minister's speech itself, I shall not follow him in all of the extraordinary mental convolutions, if I may use that term, which he has followed. I would say that his whole speech was characterized by the last four questions with which he concluded, and which he said the consumers of Canada would be asking. About that time, Mr. Speaker, one began to doubt if the consumers would even get an opportunity to say a word let alone ask a whole question. But these questions can be characterized as nothing more or less than trick questions. Indeed, while it was a lengthy and, I would say, a laboured speech, it was in fact a trick speech. When you analyse the speech and the points made by the minister and compare them with the evidence which was actually submitted -that is, such evidence as we were allowed to have brought before the committee-you will find that the facts upon which those points are based, like the facts upon which the questions are based, are not correct. It was a highly selective speech in its choice and presentation of the evidence. Rather than attempt to follow further the speech itself and the course which the minister took in dealing with this subject, I shall deal with the matter generally and answer the minister's points in the course of my own analysis of this problem.
Much has been made in the course of the discussion, both in and outside the house, of the effects which it is alleged this legislation is going to have upon the cost of living in Canada. I suggest that in the legislation before us today we can see evidence, when we view it in that light and when we ask ourselves just what effect this is going to have on the cost of living in Canada, of the government's impotence and inability to deal

Combines Investigation Act with that problem. We are presented with this bill as the government's contribution towards reducing living costs, the one and only solution offered by the government at this session, when their major responsibility should have been to take effective action to deal with this problem. Considered as a solution, as a contribution, as an answer to a problem or as anything more than shadowboxing with the cost of living, it is a sputtering and fizzling farce.
But if it were only that, if it were nothing more than that, then we could be done with it by laughing it to scorn for the poor inadequacy it is. But unfortunately, obvious though it is that this measure is intended to delude the consumer into thinking something is being done about the cost of living, of itself it will have little or no effect in that field, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has agreed. Yet it is positively a dangerous and improper piece of legislation to be enacting now because of the threat it presents to the existence and welfare of the small independent retailer. Indeed, the absence of any evidence that would justify the statement that it will reduce the cost of living, coupled with the existence of positive evidence that the legislation is desired by some of the largest and most powerful business interests in the country, and is opposed by thousands of small business men, supports the conclusion that the bill is so designed that it will accomplish nothing more effective than to increase the power and competitive advantages of the large chain and department stores at the expense of the small retailers.
As such it gives every impression that the government has produced a piece of legislation which will promote special interests and advance the welfare of some of their friends in the field of big business, without any corresponding benefit to the consumer, but to the peril and increasing disadvantage of the smaller, weaker independent retailer who is less able to take care of himself. Because we are unable to subscribe to such an unfair and prejudicial course; because we believe the independent merchant is a vital part of our economy; because we prefer a larger number of independent businesses as being in the best long-run interests of the consuming public and of the nation, as opposed to an increasing concentration of power in a small number of monopolies; because we consider this legislation ill-considered, hasty and unfair, we propose that it be not proceeded with, and I intend to move an amendment accordingly.
But first may I mention some of the more objectionable features surrounding the present legislation. In doing so I wish to
fMr. Fulton.]
emphasize that we are not taking a strong position either for or against the merits of the price maintenance system as presently practised. Indeed, one of our strongest objections to the course now being followed by the government is that resale price maintenance is being disallowed without sufficient evidence as to whether it is, in fact, harmful or beneficial in its results to the consumer. We do not know from any evidence already before us, because we were not allowed sufficient time to get evidence, just what its effect is on prices.
We did not have sufficient evidence to enable us to say whether it is desirable or undesirable in theory, let alone in its present effect on prices and upon the economy generally. But we did have available very positive evidence that the vast majority of independent retailers are fearful of the results in terms of unfair competition, loss leaders and increasing power in the hands of the big chain department stores, which will result if price maintenance is eliminated.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that one or two of the very large chain departmental stores- Eaton's is the conspicuous example-said they were opposed to the practice of price maintenance and in favour of the government's legislation. But we had no evidence that any small retailer supported Eaton's stand. As I have said, they were all genuinely concerned over the vastly increased powers which would be given to the giants such as Eaton's if the protection of price maintenance were taken away. If there were nothing else but the fact that Eaton's is in favour of the government's proposal and the little man is opposed to it, I would proceed with caution, if not with suspicion. Without going any further into the merits or demerits of price maintenance itself, I say we have not sufficient evidence to justify us in enacting this legislation eliminating price maintenance, bearing in mind that it will place the small man at the mercy of the big fellow without giving him any alternative protection.
This refusal to allow us to get evidence was persistent and extraordinary. In fact, it was such as to go a long way towards confirming my suspicion, referred to already, that this legislation is calculated to help the big fellow. Even after Eaton's had come out against price maintenance in a well publicized brief which was circulated in advance to the press, the government consistently refused to let us call any witnesses from that concern to state why they were so much in favour of the government's proposal. Not only did they refuse to allow us to call evidence from the big men-I should point out that the one

I have named is not the only one-to ask them to justify their position, but they consistently refused to allow us the time and opportunity to call witnesses from the small retail trade who desired to be heard, or to get evidence in facts and figures from the retail trade as to the results of price maintenance, which would establish whether or not the practice worked to the advantage or to the detriment of the consumer.
We are opposed to proceeding in this manner with legislation which condemns the small retailer and deprives him of his only means of protection against the chain store and the mail order department store without having had sufficient evidence to justify such a course, and particularly without having given the small retailers of Canada a fair hearing. For the retailers of Canada, Mr. Speaker, the independent merchants, will be condemned without a trial if this bill passes, because by this bill now before the house the government proposes to condemn them practically unseen and unheard.
I have spoken of the lack of evidence and the refusal of the government to grant us the opportunity to obtain evidence. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make it perfectly clear that the lack of evidence to support the proposal now before the house is in no way the fault of the official opposition. We pressed repeatedly in the committee for the right to call witnesses and to question those witnesses on all subjects, whether they were included in their brief or whether they were in their general knowledge as people with an intimate knowledge of the retail trade of Canada. But a glance at the proceedings, both in this house and in the committee, will show the inadequacy of the consideration given to this matter and the folly of passing legislation of this kind with so little evidence.
This is a big subject, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) himself, in the course of his remarks tonight, made that as one of his main points. He said: "This is not a simple subject," one of the few conclusions in which I could agree with him. It is far from a simple subject. It affects directly at least 700,000 people who are either engaged in or immediately dependent upon the retail trade of Canada. It is going to have a profound effect on every one of these people, and it may have a more considerable effect on the economy of the country generally, quite apart from its effect on the retail trade.
What consideration has, in fact, been given to this matter? What evidence do we have that there has been sufficient consideration? What evidence do we have of the facts and figures of the results that flow from the practice of resale price maintenance upon
Combines Investigation Act which we are asked to base a conclusion, and now to translate that conclusion into legislative form, absolutely outlawing and banning the practice? Well, not to go too far back-the minister went back into history, but I do not intend to follow him all the way- there has been particularly the MacQuarrie committee which is relied upon by the government as the main basis upon which they say this legislation should be enacted.
When one looks into the consideration which the MacQuarrie committee gave to this matter very serious doubts are raised as to whether that committee itself had sufficient time to give the matter the consideration it deserves, and whether they gave themselves sufficient time to justify the conclusions at which they arrived. I call to witness first the Minister of Justice to establish that the MacQuarrie committee had by no means finished their investigation when they were asked suddenly to present the interim report upon which this legislation is in the main based. Speaking in the house during this session on November 2, the minister said, as reported at page 664 of Hansard:
It therefore became clear some time ago that the MacQuarrie committee could not hope to finish its work until the end of the present calendar year at the earliest.
There is no suggestion that the MacQuarrie committee-and if there is a suggestion, there is certainly no evidence upon which the suggestion is based-had in fact completed and concluded in every way their study of the question of resale price maintenance, or of the general subject which was referred to them, when on September 10 the minister wrote them a letter in which he asked them to make a report with respect to this question of price maintenance. That report, Mr. Speaker, in spite of the fact that the minister said it was clear the MacQuarrie committee had not finished its work, was produced by October 1, just twenty days after the committee was asked to report on this matter. That report, Mr. Speaker, contains no evidence; it is nothing more than a collection of opinions; and indeed from the evidence we heard at the parliamentary inquiry into this matter, it became very doubtful as to whether or not the MacQuarrie committee had in fact received anything more than an expression of opinion. Whether they had asked for or been presented with any facts or figures upon which to make a statistical analysis which would justify them in their conclusion that price maintenance as a practice is against the best interests of the Canadian consumer is, to say the least, extremely doubtful. All that appears in their interim report is a collection of opinions, and from

Combines Investigation Act appearances they simply added up the opinions for and the opinions against and subtracted one from the other, and came to the conclusion that "the ayes had it."
That is not my own opinion only, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the adequacy of the evidence before us and its efficiency as the basis for the legislation we are now asked to pass. I would refer particularly to the opinions of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, as presented in a brief to us and as substantiated by Mr. Percy Bengough, the president of the trades and labour congress, in his evidence before the committee. The brief of the trades and labour congress, which incidentally I should say here and as will appear in more detail later as we analyse the evidence that we were allowed to get, did not take a strong position opposed to the practice of price maintenance-

That will appear more particularly later. They certainly did take a very definite position that the MacQuarrie committee's report was not a substantial basis upon which to condemn the practice. I will read from page 380 of the proceedings of the committee, where after referring to the question of whether or not the factors mentioned by the MacQuarrie committee justified their conclusions, they say:
No concrete evidence has been produced in the interim report to show the real influences in this regard and in the absence of such facts your committee is, in essence, acting in the dark.
That of course, Mr. Speaker, as it turned out, became more and more apparent the longer the committee sat; because the more it became obvious that in order for us to be able to make an intelligent conclusion on this subject we must have statistical evidence, the more determined the government became to deny us every opportunity of obtaining such evidence. The trades and labour congress brief on the same subject says as follows, as reported at page 381:
We have raised these doubts about these matters, not because we favour resale price maintenance as such, but because we are not favourably impressed with the interim report. There is an air of artificiality about the interim report. It states its case and reaches its conclusions without adducing any pertinent or concrete evidence of resale pricefixing practices in Canada. The effect of its vague and quasi-technical exposition is to suggest that it is merely a contrived argument to support a preconception.
It was upon the basis of that report, whose very form suggests that it was merely "a contrived argument to support a preconception"-and that is the considered opinion of the largest and most responsible labour organization in Canada-that the government committed itself in the speech from the throne

to introduce legislation outlawing price maintenance. And in the same speech from the throne they coupled, immediately after the undertaking to introduce this legislation, the inference that it was designed to reduce the cost of living.
Then, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar-son) himself has confirmed this afternoon, a form of second thought set in as a result of many protests from retailers affected, which the government and others began to receive. So the government decided it would appoint a joint parliamentary committee of both houses of parliament. At this moment I think I should pause to pay tribute to the chairman of that committee, who revealed himself as very able indeed. It is unfortunate that his ability was demonstrated chiefly in his success in preventing the committee from getting evidence. But he was very able in that regard.
But, Mr. Speaker, if this subject, upon which the government said in the speech from the throne that it was proposing definitely to base legislation, was thus suddenly to be referred on second thought to a parliamentary committee, one would have assumed at least that it was intended to give that committee the opportunity to study the merits of the question. After all, if the matter is referred to a committee and that committee is not given the opportunity to study the merits of the question, the only conclusion to which one could come, and the only conclusion which the facts support, is that the government appointed that committee and referred the MacQuarrie report to it for the sole purpose of enabling themselves to evade their proper responsibility, and to have the committee act as a rubber stamp of the MacQuarrie report so that the government, if taxed with its responsibility for the legislation, might be able to say, "Oh, but we referred the whole matter to a joint committee of parliament and it recommended legislation."
That is in fact all that has happened, except that the committee did not act only in the capacity of a rubber stamp. We were allowed to add to our functions that of an adding machine. We were allowed to add up the opinions, both pro and con. We were allowed to add the number of briefs in favour of price maintenance and to add the number of briefs opposed to price maintenance, and to subtract one from the other. Then, having acted as an adding machine, our functions were limited to that of rubber stamping the MacQuarrie recommendations.
Sir, I object most strenuously to this improper use of the parliamentary committee.

I object to the appointment of such a committee on the pro forma basis that it is to have referred to it a committee's report, that it is to consider that report, and then to having the committee's investigation cramped and confined and effectively gagged so that an adequate consideration, indeed any consideration, is made quite impossible.
I have referred to the lack of evidence before the MacQuarrie committee upon which conclusions could properly be based, as well as to the lack of evidence before the parliamentary committee. There were no less than six separate demands by way of substantive motions on the part of opposition members in that committee in an endeavour to obtain evidence which would enable us to reach an intelligent conclusion. Each one of those motions was voted down by the government's majority on the committee.
On two occasions those adverse votes were reversals of previous decisions the committee had arrived at. The procedure was most extraordinary. On two occasions members of the committee, as one would have expected intelligent men to do, had arrived at the conclusion that we should in fact place ourselves in possession of sufficient evidence and sufficient facts and figures surrounding this practice to enable us to reach a proper conclusion. But overnight, after an opportunity for consultation between the chairman and the government which had appointed him, efforts were made-

Will my hon. friend tell me
how it would be possible to make a comparison between identical goods sold in Canada under resale price maintenance and those not under resale price maintenance when those sold under price maintenance are sold right across Canada?

speechtext: The minister's question is about as clear as the four questions at the end of his speech. Our motion asked for a comparison of goods of comparable quality and category in Canada, both price-maintained and non-price-maintained. I think I had better read the motion so that the actual request for information will be before the house. I quote from page 301 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee as follows:

that the steering committee in conjunction with the committee counsel and the Combines Investigation Act commissioner formulate a series of questions to be put to all manufacturing groups coming before the committee; and in cases where the witnesses wish that the names of the manufacturers producing figures be kept secret, committee counsel and the Combines Investigation Act commissioner sit in with the witnesses in order to assure the committee that the figures are representative.
The minutes then record that:
After discussion, and the question having been put on the said motion, it was resolved in the affirmative.
That was the first motion, on November 26. Then, on November 27 the steering committee reported against that suggestion. In amendment to the report of the steering committee I moved the following motion, and I quote from pages 345 and 346 of the minutes of proceedings, as follows:
That for the purpose of enabling the committee to compare profit margins and cost to the consumer in both price-maintained and non-maintained goods, committee counsel together with the combines commissioner procure from manufacturers and retailers appearing before the committee (as individuals or through their association) figures for typical commodities in the lines produced or handled by them, showing the following stages in (he distributive process:
(1)	the factory cost


(2)	the price to the distributor
(3)	the price to the retailer
(4)	the price to the ultimate purchaser
for price-maintained and non-maintained goods of comparable category and quality; and that with respect to a departmental store or manufacturing concern which does its own manufacturing and distributing the figures be given with the omission of the appropriate stages outlined above;
and that counsel be empowered to employ a cost accountant as and when necessary for the purpose of such study.
After discussion and the question having been put on the said amendment, it was negatived-
There was only one member on the government side who voted for the motion, the hon. member who has been mentioned by the Minister of Justice as being very much concerned about the course proposed to be followed. I refer to the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Murray). On that occasion the committee reversed its previous decision and decided that it would not obtain evidence of either profit margins or the price to the consumer on price-maintained and non-maintained goods of comparable category and quality in Canada. This decision was reached although one of the witnesses, in fact more than one but especially Mr. Harris, president of the Canadian retail federation, a most excellent witness, advised us definitely that such a study could be made and that his organization would be glad to help in producing such evidence, that is, evidence relating not only to profit margins but to the end price to the consumer of price-maintained and non-maintained lines.
It will be seen that the committee decided definitely by that vote that it would not obtain factual evidence of the only type which would have enabled it to decide intelligently whether or not the system of pi'ice maintenance in fact operates to the detriment of the consumer with respect to prices. After all, it seems to me hardly reasonable to say the least to ask parliament to condemn a practice of such widespread nature throughout the retail trade, the elimination of which is causing such concern to independent retail merchants, without allowing us to get the facts as to whether or not the practice actually raises prices. That seems to me to be asking us to indulge in a course of legislative folly.
After the attitude which government supporters showed in the committee-government supporters led mainly by the Minister of Justice, who was a member, and by the chairman of the committee-of insisting that such evidence would be meaningless and beyond the powers of the members of the committee to apprehend, it is extraordinary to say the least, to note the same minister who said that even if we did make that

full study it could not be of any value to us, now producing the relatively infinitesimal amount of statistical information with which we have been served in the course of his speech tonight, and stating solemnly that the statistics he has quoted justify the conclusion that price maintenance operates to the disadvantage of the consumer. It is a most atrocious contradiction in attitudes. This same minister who said we could not and should not take the time to have these figures produced because we could not understand them and because they would not prove anything in any case now states, according to page 21 of the text of his remarks tonight:
These statistical data-
Based mainly on United States statistics, not Canadian.
-are sufficient to establish two generalizations that hold true, broadly if not universally, of the effect of resale price maintenance.
The minister in charge of these proceedings who told the joint committee of parliament that they should not have figures because they could not understand them and because they could not base any conclusions on them now comes solemnly into this house with two or three American figures and says that "these statistical data" are sufficient to establish the proposition that price maintenance operates to the detriment of the consumer.
The result of that extraordinary mental process and the insistence of the government majority that we were not allowed to have any adequate evidence is that the joint parliamentary committee was not and this house is not in possession of sufficient facts and figures from which to draw any conclusion that price maintenance does in fact operate to the detriment of the consumer. But as though there were not a sufficient limitation placed upon our deliberations by the refusal to allow us to get statistical figures, our deliberations were further stultified by the limitation of the time available for the consideration and study of this problem. A few figures here will, I think, suffice to demonstrate what I have said. Our sittings started on November 13 and concluded on December 7. During that time we held nineteen sittings, of which one was an organizational meeting and the last two were executive sessions. We only had sixteen sittings during which it was possible to hear evidence and examine witnesses. In that short time, sixteen sittings, we were expected to consider forty-two briefs, two supplementary briefs, three briefs by way of letter or resolution, the foregoing being, material which was laid before the committee, making quite an impressive list, in addition to many hundreds of private wires and letters received by members.
Combines Investigation Act For all that mass of information and opinion we were allowed just sixteen sittings to examine witnesses, consider the representations, discuss the problem and arrive at an intelligent conclusion on it. I am not one who shares the rather low opinion that members of the government obviously have of the capabilities of members of parliament but even I, although I do believe we could have comprehended statistical data, certainly do not set our ability so high that I would say we could arrive at an intelligent conclusion on the great volume of matters laid before us within the time which we were allowed to consider them.
In contrast to this general refusal to allow our committee to get any facts and figures on which we might base an intelligent opinion is the attitude of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that the MacQuarrie committee's conclusions must be accepted because they are a group of experts. That opinion is, I think, completely disposed of when one considers the evidence of three of the witnesses who appeared before the special committee, to the effect that the MacQuarrie committee had neither asked for nor been provided with facts and figures from the witnesses appearing before them to substantiate the simple statements of opinion which they had heard. I refer to Mr. Harris, the president of the Canadian retail federation, Mr. Preston, secretary-manager of the Canadian pharmaceutical association, both of whom said their organizations had neither been asked for nor provided any statistical data to the MacQuarrie committee, and Mr. Fred McGregor, who stated from his knowledge of the matter he considered it proper that the MacQuarrie committee had not had any such evidence
I submit that the facts I have presented establish that we have not sufficient evidence to justify the legislation outlawing price maintenance which we are now asked to endorse. On the other hand we do have evidence that it is extremely unlikely that the enactment of this legislation would have any substantial effect on the cost of living. You see, Mr. Speaker, we are being asked to embark upon this course largely as a result of political pressure which has been built up throughout the country, inspired by the government's propaganda to the effect that if this legislation is introduced the cost of living will be substantially reduced. Against that I would cite the opinion of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent), as reported at page 41 of Hansard for October 15, in the course of the throne speech debate. He said:
. . . and again I can say that as regards immediate additional measures to curb inflation, while others

Perhaps I did not understand the hon. gentlemen. I have said before that Mr. McGregor was called on the initial suggestion of members of the opposition, and 1 have no apology to make for that. But I think there is some explaining to be done on the part of the government as to why, after hearing him, they refused to allow any other witnesses to be called as requested by us.
Mr. McGregor, whose evidence is relied on to such a great extent by the government, makes it quite clear that his opposition to the practice of resale price maintenance is based entirely upon theory, and that it proceeds in no way from any conclusion or

finding of fact on his part that the practice of price maintenance operates to the detriment of the consumer by increasing prices. I refer the house to the evidence of Mr. McGregor, as reported at page 596 of the proceedings of the committee, where I asked this question:
Q. . . . then do I take it that in arriving at your conclusion that it is against the public interest-
That is, the practice of resale price maintenance.
-you divorce from your mind any consideration of whether or not in the long run it operates to reduce prices to the consumer? Do I understand you are simply saying that because it restricts competition it is adverse to the public interest?
A. That is pretty much the basis of my own thinking on it, except that I would add that not every restriction of competition should be regarded as offensive; it must be an undue restriction.
Q. Your opposition to price maintenance as set forth in your brief proceeds entirely from your proposition that it is a restriction of competition, and not at all from the basis that it affects the public adversely from the point of view of the ultimate price to the consumer?
A. Correct, undue restriction of competition is the basis in my opinion.
You therefore see, Mr. Speaker, that it is the definite and unequivocal opinion of the star witness for the government that price maintenance should be opposed not because it has any adverse effect upon prices or that it affects the consumer price-wise, but simply because of his theory that it is an undue restriction of competition.
Together with that fact, Mr. Speaker, I ask the house to consider this significant point. It is in no wise the manufacturer who is responsible for price maintenance. An attempt has been made by the government, through its propaganda, to create the impression throughout the country that this practice of resale price maintenance is brought about by powerful manufacturers' organizations seeking, to serve their own selfish interests only, to gain control over the whole Canadian economy and to grind consumers by raising prices. That is the impression they have sought to create but it is one that is most definitely at variance with the facts; because the evidence-such evidence as we were allowed to get before the committee- definitely tended the other way. Again I rely upon the evidence of Mr. McGregor in this connection, that it is not the manufacturer who wants this, that it is not even the manufacturer who benefits mostly by it, but that it is the small retailers who want it. I ask the house to consider Mr. McGregor's answer as found at page 596 of the proceedings of the committee in reply to this question:
Q. You have also I think referred to the desire of the manufacturers to have their prices main-
Combines Investigation Act tained. Now, as between the manufacturer and the retailer, who benefits most, who wants it most?
A. Unquestionably the retailers.
There was no hesitation or equivocation about Mr. McGregor's answer: Unquestionably the retailers. I therefore ask the house again, Mr. Speaker, in considering this matter, to bear in mind that such evidence as we have not only fails to establish that price maintenance has an adverse effect upon the consumer with regard to prices, or an adverse physical effect upon prices; but that there is evidence that establishes quite conclusively that it will have little or no effect in reducing the cost of living, if outlawed; and furthermore, that it is the small retailer who desires it-and designed it-as a form of self-protection and not the manufacturer who wants it to enlarge his influence.
I see that it is close to ten o'clock. I just want to lay before the house one other consideration and then the amendment which I propose to move, before adjourning the debate. The other consideration with which I wish to deal just for a moment is the question of whether or not there is adequate protection against the practice of loss leaders which are so much feared by the small retailer and by which he feels he will be knocked out if price maintenance is eliminated. The minister says: Well, we will get evidence on this matter, and if any untoward practices develop we will act to meet them. On this subject of whether or not the elimination of price maintenance by the passage of this bill will harm the small retailer the government in effect says: Wait and see. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has said: Pass the legislation and let us put it into effect; then we will take a good look at it, and if we see that it is having harmful effects on the small retailer, then we will consider some adequate form of protection. That has been said in the committee as well as implied in the house.
This surely is a most irresponsible and callous attitude for a government in charge of the administration of the nation's business to adopt. It reminds me of nothing more than the cases we so often read about in the paper, of the small boy who picks up the gun, pulls the trigger and then, when his father or brother lies dead on the floor, says: I didn't know it was loaded. But in this case the difference is that the government is deliberately pulling the trigger first, not just because they did not know it was loaded but because they had a shrewd suspicion that it was loaded but they thought this was the best way of finding out whether it would have damaging results. What they are saying is the same as if a doctor said: We do not know whether the medicine will cure or kill, but

Combines Investigation Act let us administer it to the patient anyway, whether he likes it or not; and then if he dies, we can always hold a post mortem to find out whether the cure was responsible for the death. [DOT]
For the reasons which I have outlined in part so far, Mr. Speaker, we feel that this legislation is being proceeded with without adequate consideration, that it should be given much more consideration, and that alternative methods of protecting the small retailer must be enacted simultaneously with any legislation eliminating price maintenance. I therefore propose to move,-and the motion will be seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.
Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
